current_answer: A U.S. software-developer posting study found roughly 14–15% fewer junior vacancies relative to senior vacancies after ChatGPT’s release, but it did not count hires or isolate AI as the cause. A new Census study sharpens that boundary: among matched single-location U.S. firms, occupational AI-exposure scores explain only about 1–6% of variation in reported AI use. Exposure is a warning about where AI could matter, not proof that an employer adopted it or cut jobs. Other early-career and wage findings remain mixed, and a broad U.S. tracker has not found a clear economy-wide AI job-loss footprint.

catalogue_card.question: Does an AI risk score mean your firm uses AI?
catalogue_card.text: Not reliably. A U.S. Census study found exposure scores explained only about 1–6% of variation in reported AI use across matched single-location firms. It measured adoption, not job losses.

summary: A September 2026 Census working paper links 14 occupational exposure scores to U.S. firms’ reported AI use.
Exposure positively predicts adoption but explains only about 1–6% of variation across matched single-location firms.
This does not erase the junior software vacancy warning; it limits claims that exposure-based changes were caused by observed AI use.
The new paper does not count hires, wages, layoffs or personal job risk.
uncertainty: The Census result is a cross-firm association for matched single-location U.S. firms and broad AI use, not a generative-AI-only or employment estimate.
The AI-use question changed wording in November 2025; the study analyzes both versions but cannot remove every reporting or linkage bias.
The earlier junior software result measures relative online ads, not completed hires or a causal AI effect.
